results.content:
## The PC

A desktop mini board, not a laptop: a mobile CPU (Ryzen 9 8945HX) on a mini-ITX-class board, and a mobile GPU chip
(GA106M, "RTX 3060 Laptop GPU") on a desktop PCIe card, the kind sold as a converted laptop GPU (subsystem ID
`10de:0000`, no OEM's). The model's experts live in system RAM; the GPU holds the dense layers, the KV cache and a
cache of experts (2666 of the Coder's, 1864 of UD-IQ4_XS's); the experts it does not hold are computed by the CPU
from RAM or copied to the GPU over PCIe (`--pcie-frac`). So the numbers that matter are the GPU's VRAM and memory
bandwidth, the PCIe link, the RAM's bandwidth and the CPU's cores. Read on 2026-10-03 with `lscpu`, `nvidia-smi -q`,
sysfs and `lspci`; "spec" marks a vendor figure, "measured" one measured on this PC.

**GPU**

| | |
|---|---|
| Card | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Laptop GPU, GA106M (`10de:2520`, rev a1), Ampere, compute capability 8.6; VBIOS 94.06.0F.00.AE |
| VRAM | 12288 MiB GDDR6; memory clock 7001 MHz (14 Gbps effective); 192-bit bus, 336 GB/s (spec for GA106 at 14 Gbps) |
| Cores, clocks | 30 SMs, 3840 CUDA cores (spec); graphics clock up to 2100 MHz, 1980 MHz seen under the BFCL load |
| Power | 80 W limit (default and current; the card allows 1-85 W); P0 under load; 60-64 °C at 100% load |
| PCIe link | **PCIe 4.0 x16** (16 GT/s, x16, the card's maximum; the slot can do 5.0): about 31.5 GB/s each way in theory |
| PCIe, measured | **26.8 GB/s host to device** (the engine's probe at every start, so `--pcie-frac 0.55`, the default) |
| BAR1 | 8192 MiB (less than the 12 GiB of VRAM) |
| Driver | 580.142, the official driver repacked by "FrankenDriver" for converted cards: same kernel module, plus `NVreg_RegistryDwords="RM1457588=1;"` (see `~/3060M-FrankenDriver-Linux.md`); GSP firmware on, persistence mode off, dynamic power management 3 |
| CUDA | 13.0 toolkit in the conda environment (nvcc 13.0.88, cuBLAS 13.1.1.3); the engine is built for sm_86 |

**CPU**

| | |
|---|---|
| CPU | AMD Ryzen 9 8945HX (Zen 4, mobile "HX"), 16 cores / 32 threads, 1 socket, 1 NUMA node |
| Layout | two chiplets: CCD1 = cores 0-7, CCD2 = cores 8-15; logical CPUs 16-31 are the SMT siblings of 0-15 |
| Caches | L1d 32 KiB + L1i 32 KiB per core, L2 1 MiB per core (16 MiB), L3 64 MiB (32 MiB per chiplet) |
| Vector | AVX2 and AVX-512 (F, BW, DQ, VL, CD, IFMA, VBMI, VBMI2, VNNI, **BF16**, BITALG, VPOPCNTDQ) |
| Clocks | 400-5461 MHz; measured under the BFCL load: 5083 MHz on CCD1, 4901 MHz on CCD2 |
| Power policy | `amd-pstate-epp`, governor `powersave`, energy preference `performance` |
| Strata's use | 15 expert-pool workers pinned to cores 1-15 and the host thread on core 0; SMT siblings left idle (see "Where the CPU time goes") |

**Memory**

| | |
|---|---|
| Modules | 2 x 48 GB DDR5 SO-DIMM, Crucial `CT48G56C46S5.M16B1` (manufacturer ID bank 6, 0x9B), dual rank, unbuffered, no ECC, 1.1 V |
| Channels | **dual channel**: one module on channel A, one on channel B (both slots used; the board takes up to 128 GB) |
| Speed | rated DDR5-5600 (CL46), **running at 5200 MT/s** (the 8945HX's supported maximum) |
| Bandwidth | 5200 MT/s x 8 bytes x 2 channels = **83.2 GB/s** in theory; **measured: about 55 GB/s read** (66%), see below |
| Seen by the OS | 98.8 GB (`free`), 92 GiB `MemTotal`; 2 GiB is the iGPU's carve-out (`mem_info_vram_total`) |
| Settings | swap 8 GiB file (3 MiB used); transparent huge pages `madvise`; no static huge pages |
| Page cache reads | the engine loads cached model files at 8.7-9.3 GiB/s (a single-threaded file read, not a bandwidth figure) |

Read with `sudo dmidecode -t memory` (saved as `~/dmi-memory.txt`).

**CPU memory bandwidth, measured** (2026-10-04, machine idle). A STREAM-style test in C with OpenMP
(`benchmarks/2026-10-04-3060m-membw.c`: `gcc -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -fopenmp`, AVX-512 code): three 2 GiB
arrays (far larger than the 64 MiB L3), best of 5 passes, threads pinned with `OMP_PLACES`/`OMP_PROC_BIND=close`.
Bytes are counted as STREAM counts them (what the code loads and stores):

| threads (cores) | read | write | copy | triad | memset (NT stores) | memcpy (NT stores) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (core 1) | 46.2 | 24.9 | 31.4 | 35.8 | 62.3 | 36.2 |
| 2 (cores 1-2) | 51.4 | 24.8 | 34.1 | 37.9 | 65.4 | 46.4 |
| 4 (cores 1-4) | 50.9 | 24.1 | 32.4 | 36.6 | 59.1 | 48.5 |
| 8 (cores 1-8) | 52.0 | 24.2 | 31.5 | 35.5 | 57.0 | 49.1 |
| **15 (cores 1-15, Strata's workers)** | **54.6** | 24.1 | 30.9 | 34.6 | 55.2 | 48.2 |
| 16 (all cores) | 55.5 | 24.2 | 30.8 | 34.5 | 54.5 | 47.9 |
| 32 (with the SMT siblings) | 55.3 | 24.1 | 30.6 | 34.4 | 49.3 | 47.3 |
| 8, CCD1 only (cores 0-7) | 49.7 | 23.7 | 31.3 | 35.3 | 56.2 | 48.0 |
| 8, CCD2 only (cores 8-15) | 46.4 | 23.7 | 31.2 | 35.1 | 56.7 | 48.0 |
| 8, 4 on each chiplet | **57.0** | 24.7 | 31.6 | 35.4 | 56.1 | 50.0 |

GB/s; a repeat of the 15- and 16-thread rows came within 0.7 GB/s.

- **Read, what Strata's expert workers do** (they only read weights): about **55 GB/s** with 15-16 threads, 66% of
  the 83.2 GB/s theory; at most 57.0 with 4 threads on each chiplet. One thread already reaches 46 GB/s and 2-4
  reach 51: memory, not the number of cores, is the limit.
- **One chiplet** reads 46-50 GB/s, both together 55-57: each chiplet's Infinity Fabric link nearly fills the memory
  on its own, so spreading over both adds about 10%.
- **SMT siblings add nothing** (55.3 with 32 threads vs 55.5 with 16; memset drops from 54.5 to 49.3), which agrees
  with Strata leaving them idle.
- **Plain stores count half**: `write` and the stores in `copy`/`triad` first read each cache line
  (read-for-ownership), so 24 GB/s counted is about 48 GB/s of real traffic. Non-temporal stores (glibc's
  memset/memcpy at this size) skip that: 54-65 GB/s for writing.
- For comparison on this PC: the GPU's VRAM 336 GB/s (spec), the PCIe link 26.8 GB/s measured. The experts the GPU
  does not hold are read by the CPU at most at about 55 GB/s, or copied to the GPU at 26.8 GB/s.

**Storage and network**

| | |
|---|---|
| SSD | Acer SSD N3500 1 TB (MAXIO MAP1202, DRAM-less), **PCIe 3.0 x4** (8 GT/s x4: about 3.9 GB/s in theory); root on LVM, 688 GB free |
| Measured | the engine's expert load at start: 55.4 GiB of UD-IQ4_XS experts at 2.57-2.75 GiB/s (20-22 s), 23.4 GiB of Coder experts at 1.7-2.9 GiB/s - from the SSD, or partly from the page cache; when they are all cached: 8.7-9.3 GiB/s |
| Network share | `/mnt/evox2` (SMB): 112 MB/s measured with `rsync` (59.3 GB in 8 min 24 s; 93.7 GB in 13 min 16 s); loading a model straight from it ran at 0.11 GiB/s |

**System and software**

| | |
|---|---|
| Board | "Micro Computer (HK) Tech Limited" / "Meigao Innovation Technology", product `MotherBoard Series`, board `DRFXL`, BIOS 1.14 (2025-11-13); chassis type 3 = desktop |
| iGPU | AMD Raphael (Radeon 610M class), PCIe-attached at 16 GT/s x16; not used by Strata |
| OS | Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, Linux 6.8.0-136-generic, gcc 13.3.0 |
| Python | 3.14.7 in the conda environment `strata` (`~/miniconda3/envs/strata`); BFCL in `bfcl-py312` (Python 3.12) |
| Models | Qwen3.8-Flash-Next Coder IQ1_M (2 shards, 58.4 GB) and Unsloth UD-IQ4_XS (3 shards, 93.7 GB), in `~/Documents` |

## The PC

A desktop mini board, not a laptop: a mobile CPU (Ryzen 9 8945HX) on a mini-ITX-class board, and a mobile GPU chip
(GA106M, "RTX 3060 Laptop GPU") on a desktop PCIe card, the kind sold as a converted laptop GPU (subsystem ID
`10de:0000`, no OEM's). The model's experts live in system RAM; the GPU holds the dense layers, the KV cache and a
cache of experts (2666 of the Coder's, 1864 of UD-IQ4_XS's); the experts it does not hold are computed by the CPU
from RAM or copied to the GPU over PCIe (`--pcie-frac`). So the numbers that matter are the GPU's VRAM and memory
bandwidth, the PCIe link, the RAM's bandwidth and the CPU's cores. Read on 2026-10-03 with `lscpu`, `nvidia-smi -q`,
sysfs and `lspci`; "spec" marks a vendor figure, "measured" one measured on this PC.

**GPU**

| | |
|---|---|
| Card | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Laptop GPU, GA106M (`10de:2520`, rev a1), Ampere, compute capability 8.6; VBIOS 94.06.0F.00.AE |
| VRAM | 12288 MiB GDDR6; memory clock 7001 MHz (14 Gbps effective); 192-bit bus, 336 GB/s (spec for GA106 at 14 Gbps) |
| Cores, clocks | 30 SMs, 3840 CUDA cores (spec); graphics clock up to 2100 MHz, 1980 MHz seen under the BFCL load |
| Power | 80 W limit (default and current; the card allows 1-85 W); P0 under load; 60-64 °C at 100% load |
| PCIe link | **PCIe 4.0 x16** (16 GT/s, x16, the card's maximum; the slot can do 5.0): about 31.5 GB/s each way in theory |
| PCIe, measured | **26.8 GB/s host to device** (the engine's probe at every start, so `--pcie-frac 0.55`, the default) |
| BAR1 | 8192 MiB (less than the 12 GiB of VRAM) |
| Driver | 580.142, the official driver repacked by "FrankenDriver" for converted cards: same kernel module, plus `NVreg_RegistryDwords="RM1457588=1;"` (see `~/3060M-FrankenDriver-Linux.md`); GSP firmware on, persistence mode off, dynamic power management 3 |
| CUDA | 13.0 toolkit in the conda environment (nvcc 13.0.88, cuBLAS 13.1.1.3); the engine is built for sm_86 |

**CPU**

| | |
|---|---|
| CPU | AMD Ryzen 9 8945HX (Zen 4, mobile "HX"), 16 cores / 32 threads, 1 socket, 1 NUMA node |
| Layout | two chiplets: CCD1 = cores 0-7, CCD2 = cores 8-15; logical CPUs 16-31 are the SMT siblings of 0-15 |
| Caches | L1d 32 KiB + L1i 32 KiB per core, L2 1 MiB per core (16 MiB), L3 64 MiB (32 MiB per chiplet) |
| Vector | AVX2 and AVX-512 (F, BW, DQ, VL, CD, IFMA, VBMI, VBMI2, VNNI, **BF16**, BITALG, VPOPCNTDQ) |
| Clocks | 400-5461 MHz; measured under the BFCL load: 5083 MHz on CCD1, 4901 MHz on CCD2 |
| Power policy | `amd-pstate-epp`, governor `powersave`, energy preference `performance` |
| Strata's use | 15 expert-pool workers pinned to cores 1-15 and the host thread on core 0; SMT siblings left idle (see "Where the CPU time goes") |

**Memory**

| | |
|---|---|
| Modules | 2 x 48 GB DDR5 SO-DIMM, Crucial `CT48G56C46S5.M16B1` (manufacturer ID bank 6, 0x9B), dual rank, unbuffered, no ECC, 1.1 V |
| Channels | **dual channel**: one module on channel A, one on channel B (both slots used; the board takes up to 128 GB) |
| Speed | rated DDR5-5600 (CL46), **running at 5200 MT/s** (the 8945HX's supported maximum) |
| Bandwidth | 5200 MT/s x 8 bytes x 2 channels = **83.2 GB/s** in theory; **measured: about 55 GB/s read** (66%), see below |
| Seen by the OS | 98.8 GB (`free`), 92 GiB `MemTotal`; 2 GiB is the iGPU's carve-out (`mem_info_vram_total`) |
| Settings | swap 8 GiB file (3 MiB used); transparent huge pages `madvise`; no static huge pages |
| Page cache reads | the engine loads cached model files at 8.7-9.3 GiB/s (a single-threaded file read, not a bandwidth figure) |

Read with `sudo dmidecode -t memory` (saved as `~/dmi-memory.txt`).

**CPU memory bandwidth, measured** (2026-10-04, machine idle). A STREAM-style test in C with OpenMP
(`benchmarks/2026-10-04-3060m-membw.c`: `gcc -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -fopenmp`, AVX-512 code): three 2 GiB
arrays (far larger than the 64 MiB L3), best of 5 passes, threads pinned with `OMP_PLACES`/`OMP_PROC_BIND=close`.
Bytes are counted as STREAM counts them (what the code loads and stores):

| threads (cores) | read | write | copy | triad | memset (NT stores) | memcpy (NT stores) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (core 1) | 46.2 | 24.9 | 31.4 | 35.8 | 62.3 | 36.2 |
| 2 (cores 1-2) | 51.4 | 24.8 | 34.1 | 37.9 | 65.4 | 46.4 |
| 4 (cores 1-4) | 50.9 | 24.1 | 32.4 | 36.6 | 59.1 | 48.5 |
| 8 (cores 1-8) | 52.0 | 24.2 | 31.5 | 35.5 | 57.0 | 49.1 |
| **15 (cores 1-15, Strata's workers)** | **54.6** | 24.1 | 30.9 | 34.6 | 55.2 | 48.2 |
| 16 (all cores) | 55.5 | 24.2 | 30.8 | 34.5 | 54.5 | 47.9 |
| 32 (with the SMT siblings) | 55.3 | 24.1 | 30.6 | 34.4 | 49.3 | 47.3 |
| 8, CCD1 only (cores 0-7) | 49.7 | 23.7 | 31.3 | 35.3 | 56.2 | 48.0 |
| 8, CCD2 only (cores 8-15) | 46.4 | 23.7 | 31.2 | 35.1 | 56.7 | 48.0 |
| 8, 4 on each chiplet | **57.0** | 24.7 | 31.6 | 35.4 | 56.1 | 50.0 |

GB/s; a repeat of the 15- and 16-thread rows came within 0.7 GB/s.

- **Read, what Strata's expert workers do** (they only read weights): about **55 GB/s** with 15-16 threads, 66% of
  the 83.2 GB/s theory; at most 57.0 with 4 threads on each chiplet. One thread already reaches 46 GB/s and 2-4
  reach 51: memory, not the number of cores, is the limit.
- **One chiplet** reads 46-50 GB/s, both together 55-57: each chiplet's Infinity Fabric link nearly fills the memory
  on its own, so spreading over both adds about 10%.
- **SMT siblings add nothing** (55.3 with 32 threads vs 55.5 with 16; memset drops from 54.5 to 49.3), which agrees
  with Strata leaving them idle.
- **Plain stores count half**: `write` and the stores in `copy`/`triad` first read each cache line
  (read-for-ownership), so 24 GB/s counted is about 48 GB/s of real traffic. Non-temporal stores (glibc's
  memset/memcpy at this size) skip that: 54-65 GB/s for writing.
- For comparison on this PC: the GPU's VRAM 336 GB/s (spec), the PCIe link 26.8 GB/s measured. The experts the GPU

+namespace {
+using namespace strata::prefill::mmq;
+constexpr int NE = 512, TOPK = 10, TOKENS = 4165, N = 2560, FF = 640, G = 16;
+constexpr size_t TAIL = 4096;
+const int CLASSES[] = {16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96, 112, 128};   // the engine's default; the last class takes the rest
+constexpr int NCLS = 9;
+struct Shape { const char* name; ggml_type type; int64_t rows, cols; };
+const Shape SHAPES[] = {
+    {"gate/up IQ3_XXS", GGML_TYPE_IQ3_XXS, 2 * FF, N}, {"gate/up IQ2_S", GGML_TYPE_IQ2_S, 2 * FF, N},
+    {"gate/up IQ4_XS", GGML_TYPE_IQ4_XS, 2 * FF, N},   {"gate/up IQ3_S", GGML_TYPE_IQ3_S, 2 * FF, N},
+    {"down IQ4_NL", GGML_TYPE_IQ4_NL, N, FF},          {"down Q2_0", GGML_TYPE_Q2_0, N, FF},
+    {"down IQ4_XS", GGML_TYPE_IQ4_XS, N, FF},          {"down Q8_0", GGML_TYPE_Q8_0, N, FF},
+int class_of(int rows) {
+    for (int c = 0; c < NCLS - 1; ++c) if (rows <= CLASSES[c]) return c;
+    return NCLS - 1;
+std::vector<int> zipf_counts(unsigned seed) {
+    std::vector<double> z(NE);
+    double s = 0;
+    for (int i = 0; i < NE; ++i) { z[i] = std::pow(i + 1.0, -0.8); s += z[i]; }
+    std::vector<int> ne(NE);
+    for (int i = 0; i < NE; ++i) ne[i] = (int) std::lround(z[i] / s * (double) TOKENS * TOPK);
+    std::mt19937 rng(seed);
+    std::shuffle(ne.begin(), ne.end(), rng);
+    return ne;
+struct Group { int n; int maxr, optr; size_t bi; int cls; int64_t rows; };
+float time_ms(cudaStream_t s, int reps, const std::function<void()>& f) {
+    cudaEvent_t a, b; CUDA_CHECK(cudaEventCreate(&a)); CUDA_CHECK(cudaEventCreate(&b));
+    f(); f(); CUDA_CHECK(cudaStreamSynchronize(s));
+    CUDA_CHECK(cudaEventRecord(a, s));
+    for (int i = 0; i < reps; ++i) f();
+    CUDA_CHECK(cudaEventRecord(b, s));
+    CUDA_CHECK(cudaEventSynchronize(b));
+    float ms = 0; CUDA_CHECK(cudaEventElapsedTime(&ms, a, b));
+    cudaEventDestroy(a); cudaEventDestroy(b);
+    return ms / reps;
+}  // namespace
+int main(int argc, char** argv) {
+    const char* only = argc > 1 ? argv[1] : nullptr;   // a substring of a shape's name

+    const int64_t max_rows_total = (int64_t) NE * 256;
+    for (const Shape& sh : SHAPES) {
+        if (only && !std::strstr(sh.name, only)) continue;
+        if (!supported((int) sh.type) || !fits((int) sh.type, sh.rows)) { std::printf("%s: not supported / no tile\n", sh.name); continue; }
+        const size_t eb = matrix_bytes((int) sh.type, sh.rows, sh.cols);
+        std::vector<uint8_t> w((size_t) G * eb + TAIL, 0);
+        std::mt19937 rng(7); for (size_t i = 0; i < (size_t) G * eb; ++i) w[i] = (uint8_t) rng();
+        void* dw; CUDA_CHECK(cudaMalloc(&dw, w.size())); CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(dw, w.data(), w.size(), cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));
+        // 4,096 random rows, repeated over the whole buffer
+        std::vector<float> x((size_t) 4096 * sh.cols);
+        float* dx; CUDA_CHECK(cudaMalloc(&dx, (size_t) max_rows_total * sh.cols * 4));
+        for (int64_t r = 0; r < max_rows_total; r += 4096)
+            CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemcpy(dx + r * sh.cols, x.data(), x.size() * 4, cudaMemcpyHostToDevice));
+        void* dxq; CUDA_CHECK(cudaMalloc(&dxq, q8_bytes(max_rows_total, sh.cols)));
+        quantize(dx, nullptr, dxq, (int) sh.type, sh.cols, sh.cols, max_rows_total, s);
+        float* dy; CUDA_CHECK(cudaMalloc(&dy, (size_t) max_rows_total * sh.rows * 4));
+        int32_t* dids; CUDA_CHECK(cudaMalloc(&dids, (size_t) max_rows_total * 4)); iota(dids, max_rows_total, s);
+        int32_t* dbounds; CUDA_CHECK(cudaMalloc(&dbounds, (size_t) (NE + 1 + 64 * 65) * 4));
+        CUDA_CHECK(cudaStreamSynchronize(s));
+        std::printf("== %s (%.1f MB per expert)\n", sh.name, eb / 1e6);
+        auto run_groups = [&](const std::vector<Group>& gs, int64_t total, int cls) {
+            for (const Group& g : gs) {
+                if (cls >= 0 && g.cls != cls) continue;
+                Product p;
+                p.w = dw; p.type = (int) sh.type; p.w_rows = sh.rows; p.w_cols = sh.cols; p.expert_bytes = eb;
+                p.n = g.n; p.xq = dxq; p.bounds = dbounds + g.bi; p.ids = dids; p.total_rows = total;
+                p.max_rows = g.maxr; p.opt_rows = g.optr; p.dst = dy; p.ld_dst = sh.rows;
+                ctx.run(p, s);
+        // 1. uniform experts of J rows
+        std::printf("   uniform, TOPS at J =");
+        for (int J : UJ) std::printf(" %5d", J);
+        std::printf("\n                       ");
+        for (int J : UJ) {

+            for (int g0 = 0; g0 < NE; g0 += G) {
+                gs.push_back({G, J, J, bounds.size(), 0, (int64_t) G * J});

+            for (size_t j = 0; j < order.size(); ++j) off[j + 1] = off[j] + cnt[order[j]];

+            std::vector<int32_t> bounds; std::vector<Group> gs;
+            for (size_t j0 = 0; j0 < order.size();) {

+                size_t j1 = j0;
+                while (j1 < order.size() && j1 - j0 < (size_t) G && class_of(cnt[order[j1]]) == c) ++j1;
+                std::vector<int> cs;
+                for (size_t j = j0; j < j1; ++j) cs.push_back(cnt[order[j]]);
+                std::sort(cs.begin(), cs.end());

results.content:
[TODO.md](TODO.md) item 2b: the expert products' MMQ kernels run at 6-12 TOPS at the expert shapes. The lead was
llama.cpp#21284's smaller tiles. Two premises were wrong. First, MMQ on gfx1151 does not use `sudot4`: the
vendored ggml defines `AMD_WMMA_AVAILABLE` for every gfx11 chip, and each kernel instance holds 276
`v_wmma_i32_16x16x16_iu8` instructions and no `v_dot4` (`llvm-objdump` on the gfx1151 code object of
`mmq-instance-{iq3_xxs,q2_0,iq4_nl}.cu`). `sudot4` is the path for cards without matrix cores. Second, the pinned
llama.cpp (3cf0325) is newer than #21284. It has one tile table per architecture (`mmq-config-rdna3-5.cuh`, 256
threads and I = 128 for J >= 48), and #21284's tile (128 threads, I = 64) is what the RDNA 3.0 table already uses.

**The harness** (`docs/benchmarks/2026-10-06-halo-mmq-tiles.cpp`, linking `strata_mmq.lib`; random weight bytes as in
TODO 2's harness) times each expert type two ways. "Uniform" is 512 experts of exactly J rows, groups of 16, the
tile for J: the kernel's own throughput at each tile. "Layer" is one 4,165-token layer as the engine runs it since
TODO 2a: Zipf-like rows, class-major, groups of 16 within a class, the tile for the group's median. The baseline
(`...-tiles-base.log`) showed two things. IQ3_XXS and IQ2_S (the Coder's gate/up) run *slower* at J = 128 than at
J = 112 (IQ3_XXS 9.8-9.9 against 12.5-13.1 TOPS). Most types run J = 32 no faster per operation than J = 16 (IQ4_XS
gate/up 6.5 against 7.6 TOPS). The compiler's resource report (`-Rpass-analysis=kernel-resource-usage`,
`...-mmq-registers.log`) explains both:

| VGPRs / scratch bytes per lane, default scheduler | J = 16 | J = 32 | J = 48-112 | J = 128 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| IQ3_XXS (Coder gate/up) | 195 / 0 | 256 / 16 | 191-237 / 0 | **256 / 208** |
| IQ2_S (Coder gate/up) | 256 / 28 | 186 / 0 | 213-256 / 0-56 | **256 / 132** |
| IQ4_NL, Q2_0 (Coder down) | 211 / 0 | **256 / 108** | 165-241 / 0 | 228-251 / 0 |
| IQ4_XS, IQ3_S, Q8_0 (UD-IQ4_XS) | 212-227 / 0 | **256 / 120-180** | 125-245 / 0 | 229-251 / 0 |

256 VGPRs is the most a wave32 kernel can have here; the rest spills to scratch memory. The spills do not come from
the tile's area: a thread holds J/2 accumulators whatever I is, and moving J = 32 to 256 threads / I = 128 still
spilled. They come from how LLVM's default scheduler orders the fully unrolled WMMA loop.

**What was tried** (the nine MMQ instances rebuilt with extra device flags and linked ahead of `strata_mmq.lib`;
"layer" ms per layer, 2-3 runs each, `...-tiles-variants.log`):

| ms per layer | IQ3_XXS g/u | IQ2_S g/u | IQ4_XS g/u | IQ3_S g/u | IQ4_NL down | Q2_0 down | IQ4_XS down | Q8_0 down |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| default scheduler | 28.1-28.2 | 30.9-33.7 | 25.1-25.7 | 28.4-28.5 | 15.1-15.5 | 15.3-15.6 | 10.8-11.2 | 15.6-15.8 |
| `-amdgpu-sched-strategy=iterative-minreg` (no spills, 104-239 VGPRs) | 33.0 | 39.6 | 33.3 | 33.9 | 19.5 | 17.9 | 14.6 | 20.2 |
| `-amdgpu-sched-strategy=max-memory-clause` | 26.3 | 30.8 | 24.7 | 28.6 | 15.0 | 14.8 | 11.0 | 15.9 |
| `-amdgpu-use-amdgpu-trackers=1` | 26.7 | 30.8 | 26.1 | 29.2 | 15.5 | 15.7 | 11.2 | 17.3 |
| `-unroll-threshold=50` (fixes most J = 32 spills) | 27.9 | 31.2 | 23.4 | 26.4 | 14.4 | 14.2 | 10.2 | 14.6 |
| **`-amdgpu-sched-strategy=max-ilp` (shipped)** | **25.8-25.9** | **30.1-30.7** | **22.6-23.1** | **26.4-26.8** | **14.1-14.4** | **14.1-14.3** | **10.2-10.5** | **14.8-15.0** |
| max-ilp + `-unroll-threshold=50` | 25.7-25.9 | 30.0-30.1 | 22.0-22.2 | 26.6 | 14.4 | 14.2-14.4 | 10.2 | 14.7-14.9 |
| max-ilp + the #21284 tiles (128 threads, I = 64, J >= 48) | 25.3-25.6 | 31.0-31.9 | 22.0-22.5 | 26.5-27.0 | 13.9-14.0 | 13.6-13.9 | 9.7-9.9 | 14.7-15.1 |

max-ilp is the best or within the spread of the best on every type: -8% on IQ3_XXS, -10% on IQ4_XS gate/up, -6 to -8%
on the down products. It still spills a little (IQ3_XXS 72 bytes at J = 128 instead of 208, most J = 32 cases none),
and IQ3_XXS's uniform J = 128 goes 9.8 -> 12.9 TOPS. The fewest registers (iterative-minreg) is the slowest: the

**GPU kernel speed, measured** (2026-10-06, GPU otherwise idle). The prompt path's expert products run through
llama.cpp's MMQ kernels (int8 tensor cores, `strata_mmq` in `build/`). The harness is the Halo branch's
`benchmarks/2026-10-06-halo-mmq-tiles.cpp` (AIMAX395-ROCm) ported to CUDA as
`benchmarks/2026-10-06-3060m-mmq-tiles.cu`: `hip*` renamed to `cuda*`, and no `Product::opt_rows`, which this

I measured the MMQ kernel peak on this machine with the Halo benchmark: **about 37 TOPS**. The results are in a new "GPU kernel speed, measured" part of `## The PC` in `docs/3060M.md`, just before "Storage and network". I ran it twice, and the two runs agree within 1% except IQ3_XXS at J=32–48.

**Changes needed to compile.** The original `.cpp` is HIP code and couldn't build here, so I made a CUDA copy on this branch: `docs/benchmarks/2026-10-06-3060m-mmq-tiles.cu`. Two changes:
- All `hip*` calls renamed to `cuda*`, and the device line prints `sm_86` instead of `gcnArchName`.
- I removed `p.opt_rows`. That field only exists on AIMAX395-ROCm, where the tile is chosen for the group's median expert size. This branch has no such field and always chooses the tile for the largest expert. You said to change only the copied file, so I didn't port the engine change.

  The "uniform" test is unaffected, because every expert there is the same size. The "layer" test measures this branch's own tile choice, so it isn't an exact match for the Halo setup.

The build command is in the file header. It links against `build/libstrata_mmq.a` and `build/ggml/src/libggml-base.a`, and the run takes 9 s.

**Results:**
- **Peak:** 37.2 TOPS on down IQ4_XS at 256 rows per expert. Gate/up IQ4_XS reaches 36.8. Most types reach 33–36 TOPS at J=128; IQ2_S, IQ4_NL, Q2_0 and Q8_0 reach 25–28.
- **Small tiles are slow:** J=16 gives only 6–15 TOPS. Q2_0 down is slower at J=64 than at J=48 in both runs.
- **One full layer:** 16–26 TOPS (5.3–13.9 ms), which is 66–75% of the uniform J=128 speed.
- **Against the hardware maximum:** I estimated the card's int8 tensor-core peak at 102 TOPS at the 1656 MHz measured. That figure is scaled from NVIDIA's published RTX 3090 number, not measured here. The kernels reach 36% of it.
- **Against the Halo:** its shipped `max-ilp` build is 1.7–2.2× slower per expert type on the same harness, though the tile choice differs as noted above.

**Unexplained:** the SM clock stayed at 1582–1762 MHz, not the 2100 MHz maximum. Power draw was only about 35 W against the 80 W limit, yet `nvidia-smi` reported the "SW power cap" throttle reason in every sample. The doc records this as not yet explained.

The raw output of both runs is in `docs/benchmarks/2026-10-06-3060m-mmq-tiles.log`. `.gitignore` excludes `*.log`, so committing it needs `git add -f`, which is how the logs on the Halo branch were added. Nothing is committed yet.

steps.message: Small file, only hipBLAS calls. Porting by renaming:

arguments.command: f=docs/benchmarks/2026-10-05-3060m-gemm-variants.cu && git show origin/AIMAX395-ROCm:docs/benchmarks/2026-10-05-halo-gemm-variants.cpp > $f && sed -i -e 's|#include <hip/hip_runtime.h>|#include <cuda_runtime.h>|' -e 's|#include <hipblas/hipblas.h>|#include <cublas_v2.h>|' -e 's/hipblasOperation_t/cublasOperation_t/g; s/hipDataType/cudaDataType/g; s/hipblasComputeType_t/cublasComputeType_t/g; s/hipblasHandle_t/cublasHandle_t/g; s/hipblasCreate/cublasCreate/g; s/hipblasGemmEx/cublasGemmEx/g; s/hipblasStatus_t/cublasStatus_t/g; s/HIPBLAS_/CUBLAS_/g; s/HIP_R_/CUDA_R_/g; s/hipMalloc/cudaMalloc/g; s/hipMemset/cudaMemset/g; s/hipEvent/cudaEvent/g; s/hipDeviceSynchronize/cudaDeviceSynchronize/g' $f && grep -n "hip\|HIP" $f; nvcc -O3 -arch=sm_86 $f -lcublas -o build/gemm_variants 2>&1 | head && ./build/gemm_variants

lines: +// hipBLAS GemmEx on gfx1151 across dtypes, output types, layouts and shapes: which variants the library runs fast
+#include <cuda_runtime.h>
+#include <cublas_v2.h>
+#include <cstdio>
+#include <cstdlib>
+#include <cstring>
+#include <vector>
+struct Case { const char* name; int M, N, K; cublasOperation_t opA, opB; cudaDataType in, out; cublasComputeType_t comp; };
+int main() {
+    cublasHandle_t h; cublasCreate(&h);
+    const size_t big = 64ull << 20;   // elements
+    void *A, *B, *C; cudaMalloc(&A, big * 2); cudaMalloc(&B, big * 2); cudaMalloc(&C, big * 4);
+    cudaMemset(A, 0x3C, big * 2); cudaMemset(B, 0x38, big * 2); cudaMemset(C, 0, big * 4);
+    cudaEvent_t e0, e1; cudaEventCreate(&e0); cudaEventCreate(&e1);
+    const Case cases[] = {
+        {"engine: N=3072 T=8192 K=2048, T/N, BF16->F32, 32F", 3072, 8192, 2048, CUBLAS_OP_T, CUBLAS_OP_N, CUDA_R_16BF, CUDA_R_32F, CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F},
+        {"same, FP16->F32", 3072, 8192, 2048, CUBLAS_OP_T, CUBLAS_OP_N, CUDA_R_16F, CUDA_R_32F, CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F},
+        {"same, FP16->FP16 out", 3072, 8192, 2048, CUBLAS_OP_T, CUBLAS_OP_N, CUDA_R_16F, CUDA_R_16F, CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F},
+        {"same, FP16->FP16, compute 16F", 3072, 8192, 2048, CUBLAS_OP_T, CUBLAS_OP_N, CUDA_R_16F, CUDA_R_16F, CUBLAS_COMPUTE_16F},
+        {"same, BF16->BF16 out", 3072, 8192, 2048, CUBLAS_OP_T, CUBLAS_OP_N, CUDA_R_16BF, CUDA_R_16BF, CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F},
+        {"N/N layout, FP16->F32", 3072, 8192, 2048, CUBLAS_OP_N, CUBLAS_OP_N, CUDA_R_16F, CUDA_R_32F, CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F},
+        {"N/N layout, FP16->FP16", 3072, 8192, 2048, CUBLAS_OP_N, CUBLAS_OP_N, CUDA_R_16F, CUDA_R_16F, CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F},
+        {"square 4096^3, T/N, FP16->F32", 4096, 4096, 4096, CUBLAS_OP_T, CUBLAS_OP_N, CUDA_R_16F, CUDA_R_32F, CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F},
+        {"square 4096^3, N/N, FP16->FP16", 4096, 4096, 4096, CUBLAS_OP_N, CUBLAS_OP_N, CUDA_R_16F, CUDA_R_16F, CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F},
+        {"square 4096^3, T/N, BF16->BF16", 4096, 4096, 4096, CUBLAS_OP_T, CUBLAS_OP_N, CUDA_R_16BF, CUDA_R_16BF, CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F},
+        {"expert gate/up: N=1280 T=160 K=2560, T/N, FP16->F32", 1280, 160, 2560, CUBLAS_OP_T, CUBLAS_OP_N, CUDA_R_16F, CUDA_R_32F, CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F},
+        {"expert down: N=2560 T=160 K=640, T/N, FP16->F32", 2560, 160, 640, CUBLAS_OP_T, CUBLAS_OP_N, CUDA_R_16F, CUDA_R_32F, CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F},
+        {"expert gate/up, FP16->FP16", 1280, 160, 2560, CUBLAS_OP_T, CUBLAS_OP_N, CUDA_R_16F, CUDA_R_16F, CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F},
+        {"decode-like: N=3072 T=8 K=2048, T/N, FP16->F32", 3072, 8, 2048, CUBLAS_OP_T, CUBLAS_OP_N, CUDA_R_16F, CUDA_R_32F, CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F},
+    const float alpha = 1.f, beta = 0.f;
+    for (const Case& c : cases) {
+        const int lda = c.opA == CUBLAS_OP_T ? c.K : c.M, ldb = c.opB == CUBLAS_OP_N ? c.K : c.N;
+        auto run = [&]() {
+            return cublasGemmEx(h, c.opA, c.opB, c.M, c.N, c.K, &alpha, A, c.in, lda, B, c.in, ldb, &beta, C, c.out, c.M,
+                                    c.comp, CUBLAS_GEMM_DEFAULT);
+        cublasStatus_t st = run(); cudaDeviceSynchronize();
+        if (st != CUBLAS_STATUS_SUCCESS) { std::printf("%-55s status %d\n", c.name, (int) st); continue; }
+        const int reps = c.N <= 160 ? 200 : 10;
+        for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) run();
+        cudaEventRecord(e0); for (int i = 0; i < reps; ++i) run(); cudaEventRecord(e1); cudaEventSynchronize(e1);
+        float ms = 0; cudaEventElapsedTime(&ms, e0, e1); ms /= reps;
+        std::printf("%-55s %8.3f ms  %6.1f TFLOP/s\n", c.name, ms, 2.0 * c.M * c.N * c.K / (ms * 1e-3) / 1e12);
+    return 0;

steps.reasoning_content: I found the "compute 16F" row (661 TFLOP/s) is bogus because cuBLAS reads alpha/beta as `__half` under `CUBLAS_COMPUTE_16F`, so the float 1.0f gets read as half 0 and the GEMM is skipped (hipBLAS has the same issue, so the original has this bug too). I'll fix the copy by passing `__half` scalars for that case, then rerun it 3 times to check whether case order affects results since early rows may be slow from clock ramp-up.

arguments.description: Fix half scalars, rebuild, run three times with clock log

results.content:
The work list, in the order of the time at stake: the expert GEMMs (2.9 s with their dequant: a grouped GEMM or
a fixed MMQ), the prompt attention on gfx11 WMMA (1.9 s), the dense GEMMs' library efficiency (4 TFLOP/s against
the card's matrix-core peak), the GDN recurrence (0.8 s; llama.cpp's chunked form gained it 8% of a whole prompt
on this card).

## A better GEMM: what was searched, what was measured, what it gave (2026-10-05, evening)

**First, the clock.** A search turns up a Windows Strix Halo problem that would explain a 4 TFLOP/s GEMM
outright: the GPU drops to ~600 MHz for compute whenever the console display is off (lid closed, display
timeout), FP16 GEMM 31 -> 8 TFLOPS ([ROCm/legacy-rocm-build #6675](https://github.com/ROCm/legacy-rocm-build/issues/6675);
workarounds: `SetThreadExecutionState(ES_DISPLAY_REQUIRED)` in the process, or an injected 1-pixel mouse move).
This PC is driven over RDP with a 4K panel on the 8060S and a 300 s display timeout. Measured with
`docs/benchmarks/2026-10-05-halo-hip-clock.hip` (the 20-bit `SHADER_CYCLES` register over 100 us windows of the
100 MHz wall clock; gfx11 has no `s_memtime`, so `clock64()` reads 0): **2,780-2,900 MHz** under a spin load,
2,240-2,950 MHz while the hipBLASLt GEMM probe ran. Not throttled here, and the benchmark rows measured minutes
apart agree with each other. The risk stays for unattended runs longer than the display timeout; the engine does
not hold a display request.

**Second, the library, by variant** (`docs/benchmarks/2026-10-05-halo-gemm-variants.cpp`: `hipblasGemmEx` on
constant nonzero data, 10 timed calls, `ROCBLAS_USE_HIPBLASLT=1`; rocBLAS alone is 20-45% lower on every row):

| shape, layout, types | TFLOP/s |
|---|---|
| the engine's dense shape N=3072 T=8192 K=2048, T/N, **BF16 or FP16 in -> FP32 out** | **4.3** |
| the same, FP16 -> FP16 out, or BF16 -> BF16 out | **23.6-24.0** |
| N/N layout, FP16 -> FP32 / FP16 -> FP16 | 5.3 / 20.3 |
| 4096^3, FP16 -> FP32 / FP16 -> FP16 / BF16 -> BF16 | 4.3 / 25.4 / 26.1 |
| the expert shape N=1280 T=160 K=2560, FP16 -> FP32 / FP16 -> FP16 | 3.5 / 18.7 |
| the expert down shape N=2560 T=160 K=640, FP16 -> FP32 | 3.7 |
| decode-like N=3072 T=8 K=2048, FP16 -> FP32 | 1.0 |

So the slow path is one thing: **a 32-bit output**. With a 16-bit output the same library runs 5-6x faster on this
card, 24-26 TFLOP/s, which is the 32-37 TFLOP/s others measure on gfx1151 with hipBLASLt on big shapes
([llm-tracker](https://llm-tracker.info/AMD-Strix-Halo-(Ryzen-AI-Max+-395)-GPU-Performance): 36.9 peak, "59.4
theoretical"), less the FP32 accumulate and this shape. Every `cublasGemmEx` the engine issues asks for FP32 out
(`gemm.cu:388/407`), because the consumers accumulate into FP32 (`beta`, the hi/lo split GEMMs). A 16-bit output
with a cast would cap those at 11 bits: a numerical change for the maintainers, not a setting. `hipBLASLt`'s
`compute 16F` variant is faster still on rocBLAS (17 TFLOP/s) but accumulates in FP16: 1.2e-2 relative error
against 3.3e-4, unusable here. Checked with `docs/benchmarks/2026-10-05-halo-gemm-f16out.cpp` on random data.

**Third, the engine's own answer to this: its hipBLASLt solution table.** `tools/hip/tune_hipblaslt` asks
hipBLASLt for every heuristic solution of each of the engine's 32 dense GEMM shapes (T = 4096 and 8192), times
them against `hipblasGemmEx`, checks them against it (finite, max abs, relative L2 tolerances) and writes the
best ids. On gfx1151 with hipBLASLt 1.4.1 (60 s): **every shape found a 5.2-5.4x faster solution with FP32
output** (f16 T=8192 N=12288 K=2560: 201.0 -> 38.4 ms, 2.6 -> 13.4 TFLOP/s; T=4096: 101.5 -> 18.9 ms; the
96x96x32 macro-tile `SAV` kernels), shipped as `tools/hip/gfx1151-hipblaslt-100401.txt` (setup uses it when the
installed hipBLASLt reports 1.4.1; the configs here carry `STRATA_HIPBLASLT_TUNING`). The engine with the table:

| Coder IQ1_M, arena mode (the first two columns at 64/64, the table column at 32/96: the split the BIOS was left on after the UD-IQ4_XS runs; the cache held all 12,288 experts and hit 100% in every run either way) | plain | `ROCBLAS_USE_HIPBLASLT=1` | **the table** (+ the switch for the shapes it lacks) |
|---|---|---|---|
| pp4096 (`pp4k.py`, 2 requests) | 199-207 t/s | 264-279 t/s | **404-452 t/s** |
| 4,165-token prompt, GPU timeline | 19,955 ms | 14,725 ms | **9,188 ms** |
| hc read / GDN projections / QSA proj / router | 3,438 / 4,969 / 2,077 / 909 ms | 1,768 / 3,263 / 1,443 / 591 | **673 / 938 / 468 / 274** |
| QSA attn / expert GEMMs gate-up + down / dequant | 1,986 / 1,772 + 785 / 489 | 1,944 / 1,705 + 763 / 473 | 2,034 / 1,803 + 798 / 482 (untouched: not in the table) |
| the benchmark, prefill @ 4.75K / pp4096 / 16K prefix / 20K | 209 / 209 / 213 / 211 | 274 / 268 / 277 / 274 | **451 / 441 / 440 / 434 t/s** |
| the benchmark, decode (cold / fresh / after 4.75K / tg128 @ 16K) | 35.0 / 33.0 / 31.3 / 27.5 | 38.6 / 35.1 / 34.7 / 28.8 | 39.9 / 36.1 / 30.9 / 29.2 |

So the slow path is one thing: **a 32-bit output**. With a 16-bit output the same library runs 5-6x faster on this

([llm-tracker](https://llm-tracker.info/AMD-Strix-Halo-(Ryzen-AI-Max+-395)-GPU-Performance): 36.9 peak, "59.4

arguments.new_string:
(`AIMAX+395-ROCm.md` on that branch); here 10.9-13.9 and 5.3-8.5 ms, 1.7-2.2 times faster per type (the tile choice differs, see above).

**cuBLAS GEMM speed, measured** (2026-10-06, GPU otherwise idle). The Halo branch's
`benchmarks/2026-10-05-halo-gemm-variants.cpp` (`GemmEx` across input/output types, layouts and shapes, constant
nonzero data, 10 timed calls, 200 for the small shapes) ported to cuBLAS as
`benchmarks/2026-10-05-3060m-gemm-variants.cu`: `hip*` renamed, and the `compute 16F` row given `__half`
alpha/beta (cuBLAS reads them in the compute type; with the original's float 1.0 it read 0, skipped the product and
reported 661 TFLOP/s). Three runs back to back (`benchmarks/2026-10-06-3060m-gemm-variants.log`); the table gives
runs 2-3, as run 1's first three rows were still on a rising clock (20.3-23.7 TFLOP/s). SM clock 1935-2017 MHz.

| shape, layout, types | 3060M TFLOP/s | Halo (gfx1151, hipBLAS + hipBLASLt) |
|---|---|---|
| the engine's dense shape N=3072 T=8192 K=2048, T/N, **BF16 or FP16 in -> FP32 out** | **28.0-28.1** | 4.3 |
| the same, FP16 -> FP16 out / BF16 -> BF16 out | 29.0-29.1 / 28.8-29.0 | 23.6-24.0 |
| the same, FP16 -> FP16, compute 16F (FP16 accumulate) | 37.4-38.6 | - |
| N/N layout, FP16 -> FP32 / FP16 -> FP16 | 27.7-27.8 / 28.3 | 5.3 / 20.3 |
| 4096^3, T/N FP16 -> FP32 / N/N FP16 -> FP16 / T/N BF16 -> BF16 | 26.6-26.7 / 27.4-27.5 / 28.2 | 4.3 / 25.4 / 26.1 |
| the expert shape N=1280 T=160 K=2560, FP16 -> FP32 / FP16 -> FP16 | 22.2 / 21.8-22.2 | 3.5 / 18.7 |
| the expert down shape N=2560 T=160 K=640, FP16 -> FP32 | 10.6 | 3.7 |
| decode-like N=3072 T=8 K=2048, FP16 -> FP32 | 2.0 | 1.0 |

- **No FP32-output penalty here**: FP32 out runs at 96-97% of 16-bit out on the engine's shape (28.0 vs 29.0),
  where the Halo's hipBLAS loses 5-6x. Every `cublasGemmEx` the engine issues asks for FP32 out, so this card needs
  no tuning table for it.
- **The library is near the card's limit**: GeForce Ampere does FP16/BF16 with FP32 accumulate at 512 operations
  per clock per SM (from NVIDIA's RTX 3090 figure: 71 TFLOPS, 82 SMs, 1695 MHz), 30.4 TFLOP/s for 30 SMs at
  1980 MHz. 28-29 TFLOP/s is 92-95% of that. FP16 accumulate is twice the rate (60.8); 37-39 TFLOP/s measured,
  and the Halo branch found FP16 accumulate too inexact for the engine (1.2e-2 relative error against 3.3e-4).
- **The small shapes take 47-51 us each** whatever their size: the expert gate/up (1.05 GFLOP) 22 TFLOP/s, the
  down (0.52 GFLOP) 10.6, decode-like (0.10 GFLOP) 2.0. The decode-like call reads 12.6 MB of weights in 50 us,
  252 GB/s, 75% of the VRAM's 336 GB/s.
- Against the int8 MMQ above (37 TOPS at best, 16-26 TOPS per layer): the FP16 GEMM at an expert's shape gives
  22 TFLOP/s, but the engine's experts stay quantized for MMQ, which reads each 0.5-1.7 MB expert once instead of a
  dequantized FP16 copy.

**Storage and network**

steps.message:
I ran `2026-10-05-halo-gemm-variants.cpp` on this card. It's now a new part of `## The PC` in `docs/3060M.md`, "cuBLAS GEMM speed, measured", with the Halo's numbers next to mine.

**The copy:** `docs/benchmarks/2026-10-05-3060m-gemm-variants.cu`. Renaming `hip*` to `cu*` compiled cleanly, but one row came out wrong. For the `compute 16F` case, cuBLAS reads alpha/beta as `__half`. The original passes a float 1.0, which cuBLAS read as 0, so it skipped the multiply and reported 661 TFLOP/s. I pass `__half` values for that case only; the build command and this note are in the file header.

I ran it 3 times back to back. In run 1 the first three rows were 20–23 TFLOP/s because the clock was still ramping up. Runs 2 and 3 agree within 1–3%, and the table uses those. The SM clock was 1935–2017 MHz during the GEMMs.

**Results:**

| Engine's shape N=3072 T=8192 K=2048 | 3060M | Halo |
|---|---|---|
| BF16/FP16 in → FP32 out | **28.0** TFLOP/s | 4.3 |
| FP16 → FP16 out | 29.0 | 23.6–24.0 |
| FP16 accumulate (compute 16F) | 37.4–38.6 | – |

- **No penalty for FP32 output here.** FP32 out runs at 96–97% of the speed of 16-bit out. On the Halo, FP32 out is 5–6× slower, which is why it needed its hipBLASLt tuning table. This card doesn't.
- **cuBLAS is close to the card's limit.** 28–29 TFLOP/s is 92–95% of the FP16 tensor-core peak with FP32 accumulate (30.4 TFLOP/s at 1980 MHz). I scaled that peak from NVIDIA's published RTX 3090 figure; it isn't measured here.
- **Small shapes all take 47–51 µs, whatever their size:**
  - expert gate/up: 22 TFLOP/s
  - expert down: 10.6 TFLOP/s
  - decode-like: 2.0 TFLOP/s, i.e. 252 GB/s of weight reads, 75% of the VRAM's 336 GB/s

The raw output is in `docs/benchmarks/2026-10-06-3060m-gemm-variants.log`. Like the MMQ log, it is excluded by `.gitignore` and needs `git add -f` to commit. Nothing is committed yet.

arguments.description: Map Strata's decode path on 3060M
arguments.prompt:
Read-only research. Do NOT modify any files. Repository: /home/luwei/work/AI/Strata (branch 3060M), a C++/CUDA engine running the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next MoE model (Coder IQ1_M and Unsloth UD-IQ4_XS variants) on one GPU plus system RAM. This PC: RTX 3060 Laptop GPU 12 GB (336 GB/s VRAM), PCIe 4.0 x16 measured 26.8 GB/s H2D, Ryzen 9 8945HX 16 cores, 96 GB DDR5-5200 dual channel measured ~55 GB/s read. Experts live in system RAM; the GPU caches some experts (2666 of the Coder's, 1864 of UD-IQ4_XS's); the rest are computed on CPU or copied over PCIe (--pcie-frac).

I need a fact sheet about Strata's decode and prefill speed on THIS machine and what speed features it already has, so someone can judge which optimizations from another project could be ported. Sources: docs/3060M.md (the main one for this machine: measured tokens/s, where the time goes, CPU time breakdown, pcie-frac A/B), docs/DETAILS.md (engine design, every measured number, settings), docs/TODO.md if present, and src/ / include/ as needed.

Report:
1. Measured decode tokens/s and prefill tokens/s on this 3060M machine for each model, with the settings, and the breakdown of where decode time goes per token (GPU dense layers, CPU experts, PCIe copies, attention, sampling, sync), with the doc and line.
2. Whether Strata has speculative decoding: MTP head (multi-token prediction), a draft model ("drafter", look for E-9, "drafter", "speculative", "mtp", "draft" in src, include, docs), n-gram/prompt lookup, etc. If yes: how it works, acceptance rate, measured gain, whether it's on by default, and how verification of K draft tokens is batched (does verifying K tokens cost about the same as 1 token in the expert/CPU path, or K times, given that different tokens route to different experts?). Does the Flash-Next GGUF contain MTP layers and does Strata load them?
3. How Strata handles the linear-attention (GDN / gated delta net) recurrent state, and whether it has state rollback/checkpointing for rejected drafts.
4. Other speed features already present: expert cache policy, CPU expert kernels (AVX-512 etc.), MMQ, CUDA graphs, fusions, KV cache type, prompt cache / disk cache, multi-slot.
5. Known bottlenecks / open TODO items for decode speed on this machine.

Return a structured markdown report, at most about 1,500 words, with file:line citations; mark measured vs unmeasured.

  # Speed optimizations in rulith-inference: a catalogue
  
  **Sources and conventions.** Paths are relative to `/mnt/evox2/large/work/AI/rulith-inference`. `MAN:n` means `patches/MANIFEST.md` line n, `RES:n` means `docs/results.md` line n, `27B:n` means `docs/Qwen3.8-27B.md` line n. Numbers are quoted as the docs give them. Everything is measured on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395 / gfx1151 under Windows, unless a row says otherwise. **[M]** means measured. **[C]** means a claim or static analysis with no measurement. "FN" is Flash-Next (arch `qwen4exp`, 125B-A6B, 512 experts with 10 active, the UD-IQ4_XS file). "27B" is the dense `qwen35`. Almost all kernel work is HIP code inside ggml-cuda. Several kernels are marked RDNA3.5-only, and most of the graph work is specific to qwen4exp.
  
  ## 1. Where decode time goes (`docs/decode-budget.md`)
  
  This was measured at 85K context with MTP on, per speculative pass. A pass yields 2.7–2.9 accepted tokens (decode-budget.md:3-16) **[M]**:
  
  - **Pass: 86 ms**
    - Target verify, 1+3 tokens: **69 ms**
      - Host: 10.3 ms (prep 1.5, graph 1.8, set_inputs 1.3, submit 5.7)
      - Device: about 58 ms, of which **about 43 ms is weight bandwidth**
    - 3 draft steps: 13 ms, about 4.3 ms each
      - LM head 2.4 ms
      - 85K draft KV read 0.8 ms
      - MTP layer 0.65 ms
    - Catch-up 1 ms, sampling 0.5 ms, other 1.6 ms
  
  Other measured points in the same file:
  
  - **Expert bytes per token.** 1.16 GB of expert weights are read per token (:20-22).
  - **Host overlap.** The host's 4.6 ms ahead of submit does not overlap the GPU (:24).
  - **Re-measured 2026-09-21** (:55-65):
    - A bare target graph takes 69 / 97 / 140 / 202 ms for 4 / 8 / 16 / 32 tokens.
    - Fusions are worth about 10 ms at 4 tokens (2473 dispatches).
    - About 42 ms is bytes at the ceiling: 4.64 GB of Q8_0 trunk plus about 4.4 GB of experts at about 204 GB/s.
    - About 22–27 ms is everything else.
  - **Step cost model.** A step costs about 30 ms plus about 1 ms per distinct expert touched. Distinct experts are 10 / 39 / 76 / 139 / 238 for 1 / 4 / 8 / 16 / 32 tokens (:94-95).
  - **MTP-off token** (RES:753-755): about 5.84 GB of weights (trunk 4.68 GB plus experts 1.16 GB). The bandwidth floor is about 27.8 ms at about 210 GB/s, against 37.0 ms measured at 3K.
  
  ## 2. MTP / speculative decoding
  
  **Does FN have MTP layers?**
  - FN does **not** use an embedded MTP head. It drafts with Unsloth's separate `mtp-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-shared-Q4_K_M.gguf` (1.9 GB), passed with `-md` (README:64).
  - The manager excludes qwen4exp from embedded MTP on purpose (tools/manager.py:612-616; 27B:155).
  - The draft layer's tensors are named `blk.48.nextn.*`; a mismatched draft fails with `blk.48.nextn.hc_head_norm.weight not found` (GMKtec_EVO-X2.md:72).
  - I did not find a statement on whether FN's main GGUF itself carries `nextn` tensors.
  - The 27B has one embedded NextN layer (`nextn_predict_layers` 1) and uses `--spec-type draft-mtp` with no `-md` (27B:9, 35).
  
  **Overall gain and acceptance [M]**
  
  | Model / setting | Without MTP | With MTP | Acceptance / draft | Source |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | FN, 85K | 21.5 tok/s | 34.9 tok/s (draft head + 3 drafts + n-gram off) | — | README:120 |
  | FN, 20K | 22.3 tok/s | 38.7 tok/s (+74%) | — | install.md:261 |
  | FN, 0.4.0 headline, 86K | — | 23.9 ms/token = 41.8 tok/s | 65%, 2.90 tokens/pass | RES:34 |
  | FN, 0.4.0 headline, short context | — | 21.7 ms/token | 65%, 2.88 tokens/pass | RES:35 |
  | FN, Chinese prose (older build) | — | — | 68–69% | RES:97-98 |
  | 27B (EngramHalo comparison run) | 12.4 t/s | 31.5 t/s (2.5×), EngramHalo 24.6 | 89.8–92.0% | 27B:95-106 |
  | 27B, app default after P1 | 12.3 tok/s | 34.4 tok/s | — | 27B:251 |
  | 27B, 8 conversations after P1 | 51.4 tok/s | 78.4 tok/s | — | 27B:251 |
  
  - README:64 also says "~+60% decode" for FN **[C]**, with no measurement next to it.
  - The FN MTP-off headline is 27.5 / 27.0 / 26.5 tok/s at 3K / 50K / 110K (RES:39).
  - For the 27B on Chinese prose, acceptance is only 30–50% (27B:206).
  
  **Draft length**
  - FN: `draft_max` 3 gives 27.9 ms/token, 4 gives 28.7, and 5 gives 30.2 (decode-budget.md:43-47) **[M]**.
  - The reason is that MoE verify cost grows with batch size. One more draft position costs 18.5 ms (7.4 for the draft step plus 11.2 for expert bandwidth) and must return 0.64 accepted tokens; position 4 returns 0.56 (:29-41).
  - 27B (dense): the default stays 3/0.3. On code, 4–5 drafts are about 7% faster; on Chinese, 3 is best (27B:193-206). Dense verify is nearly free, so the 27B drafts at every slot count (27B:228).
  - Drafts are capped by how many slots are generating:
    - Greedy FN: `3,2,2,2,0` (RES:366, MAN:455). Four conversations went 37.9 → 47.4 tok/s.
    - Sampled FN: `2,2,1,1,0` (RES:913).
    - 27B: `dm,dm,dm,dm,dm` greedy and `3,3,3,3,2` sampled (27B:158-161).
  
  **MTP patches**
  
  | Patch | What it does | Models | Measured gain |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `make_draft_head.py` (tool, not a patch) | Gives the draft its own IQ4_XS output projection. | FN | +5% English, +9% Chinese, acceptance unchanged (RES:157; decode-budget.md:69-73) [M]. A Q4_K_M draft body beats Q8_0 by under 1% and saves 880 MB (:75). |
  | `apply_mtp_lowrank_head` (MAN:712) | A rank-512 pre-score (`lr_proj` F16 2560→512, `lr_scores` Q8_0 512→vocab) picks `STRIX_MTP_LR_K`=512 candidates. Only those rows of the target's Q6_K head are multiplied; the rest are set to -inf. | FN | The head drops from 338 MB (IQ4_XS) to 135 MB. Top-1 recall is 99.98–100% (99.90% on held-out conversations), against 96.5–97% for the IQ4_XS head. Decode at draft 2/0: greedy 42.6 → 44.2 tok/s, sampled 42.0 → 44.0. Acceptance 0.705 = 0.705 greedy and 0.687 → 0.702 sampled. Greedy output is bit-identical. No gain at 21K (RES:1049-1058) [M]. README:66 gives "+3.6–4.9%". |
  | `apply_qwen35_dense_mtp_049` (MAN:732) | The same low-rank trick for the 27B, through a side file (`STRIX_EXTRA_TENSORS`). | 27B | The head drops from 1.04 GB to 140 MB. Draft time per pass 22–24 → 11.5–12 ms; pass 119–125 → 109–116 ms. Code +10%, zh +5%, sampled +11%, acceptance unchanged. Rank 512 recall at K=512 is 99.70% (27B:274-302) [M]. |
  | `apply_mtp_index_share_031` (MAN:578; RES:653-669) | The draft layer used to attend densely to its whole cache (0.9 ms per step at 86K, 2.5 at 212K). Now a draft step reuses the sparse selection the catch-up kept, plus the cells of every position since. The indexer reruns only when the selection is more than 32 positions stale and the view is at least 32K cells. Store-only catch-ups build no attention. | FN only (needs QSA) | Pass at 86K 79.75 → 76.90 ms; at 212K 93.70 → 87.60 ms; at 30K 71.3 → 70.9; same acceptance [M]. Running the indexer in every catch-up cost 4% at about 4K. |
  | `apply_spec_sampling_042` (MAN:660; RES:892-914) | Leviathan/Chen speculative sampling for temperature > 0: drafts are drawn from q and accepted with probability min(1, p/q). | Generic server code | First-position acceptance 63.4 → 66.9%, second 58.0 → 60.0%. One conversation 33.6 → 36.2 tok/s; three conversations 61.3 → 67.1 [M]. |
  | `apply_spec_even_drafts` (MAN:478; RES:326-336) | All conversations in a step get drafts of the same length. Uneven drafts had split the verify into several full passes. | FN (hybrid memory) | Three conversations at 4K: 34.3 → 45.7 tok/s [M]. |
  | `apply_mtp_carry_state` (MAN:457) | Keeps the drafter's carried target hidden row through checkpoints, the RAM and disk tiers, and rewinds. | Both | A correctness fix (deterministic drafts after a rewind). No speed number. |
  | `apply_cache_ram_and_mtp` (MAN:274-290) | The prompt cache persists from buffers and `--cache-ram` can be lowered. An entry saved with MTP on now loads with MTP off. | Server | Resident memory 8.07 → 4.13 GB. The 79K-token conversation needs 17.3 s of prefill instead of 96.6 s cold. Turning MTP off no longer aborts the server [M]. |
  | `apply_graph_key_shape` | Puts the graph shape into the HIP graph cache key. | Generic | +2%, and draft graphs replay (RES:158) [M]. |
  | `apply_small_batch_decode`, `apply_verify_small_products`, `apply_small_m_mmvf` (MAN:498, 507, 264-271) | Verify-step products of 5–32 columns run on the vector kernel in chunks instead of MMQ, MMB or cuBLAS tiles. | FN shapes, HIP | A 9-token verify 120–123 → 103–104 ms, then 106.4 → 103.0; a 16-token pass 139.8 → 130.4 ms [M]. |
  | `apply_mmvq_i8_036` / `_unroll_037` (MAN:625, 639) | 5–8 column q8_0 / Q6_K GEMVs with a lane-contiguous activation layout. | RDNA3.5 only | 1.0–1.4 ms less per step; the Q6_K lm head 3.75 → 2.9–3.1 ms; 26.3 → 22.1 µs [M]. |
  
  **Does the MTP gain depend on weights being in fast memory?**
  - Pinned system memory reads at 229–232 GB/s, against 236 GB/s from the carve (RES:1024-1026).
  - With 32 layers' experts (37 GiB) in system memory, MTP decode was 40.39 / 41.41 against 39.56 / 40.67 tok/s, about 2% slower, at identical acceptance (RES:1014-1017) [M].
  - What hurt was the driver spilling the KV cache and compute buffers into shared memory: the 64 GB carve was 28% slower (README:132; dead-ends.md:224-227).
  - The mechanism of the gain is bandwidth: each extra verified token reads about 10 more experts (decode-budget.md:29-41).
  - The docs contain nothing about discrete GPUs or PCIe.
  
  **How MTP interacts with the GDN recurrent state**
  - **Old behaviour.** Verify wrote a 3 MB-per-layer-per-sequence state snapshot after every token so that rejected drafts could be rolled back.
  - **`apply_gdn_deferred_rollback`** (MAN:527; RES:464-475) leaves the state in place and records per token the delta, key and gate (33 KB). The next batch replays the kept records. Output is bit-identical.
    - FN verify: 9 tokens 98.85 → 96.05 ms (-2.8%); 12 tokens 119.4 → 114.6 ms (-4.0%); 4 tokens unchanged [M].
    - Ported to the 27B: verify 3–7% shorter; one conversation 89.5 vs 92.5 ms (27B:311-320) [M].
  - **`apply_gdn_records_041`** (MAN:651) lets records accumulate (W=8), so the state is written once in nine tokens, MTP off too, and a warp reads two columns. Eight conversations: step 4.6 ms shorter (82.5 → 77.9) and 87.6 → 84.4 ms [M].
  - **`apply_gdn_direct_rows`** (MAN:467) reads the rollback snapshot rows in place instead of gathering 3 MB per sequence per layer. No isolated number.
  - **`apply_state_copy_trim`** (MAN:353-357) copies the conv-state tail per rollback slot directly: 144 fewer dispatches, verify 59.40 → 58.90 ms [M].
  - The draft's own memory has no recurrent layers (MAN:651).
  - A GDN state cannot be rewound by one token, so resends restore from checkpoints (RES:1187-1190).
  
  ## 3. Other decode optimizations [M]
  
  - **QSA block-key cache** (FN): 97K decode 63.5 → 58.5 ms/token (RES:155).
  - **Sparse attention gather at decode** (FN): 58.9 → 47.9 ms/token; context slope 0.188 → 0.078 ms per 1000 tokens (RES:156).
  - **`apply_fa_gather_037`** (FN, HIP), which reads selected cells in place:
    - Eight conversations, MTP off: 99.9 → 93.6 ms per step.
    - One conversation at 50K: 38.7 → 38.0 ms.
    - MTP on with three / four streams: +2% / +3% (MAN:638).
  - **`apply_idx_score_dec_034` plus `apply_qsa_runs_034`** (FN):
    - One conversation at 110K: 45.4 → 43.1 ms.
    - Eight conversations: step 131 → 107.5 ms.
    - MTP-off slope 0.072 → 0.027 ms per 1000 tokens (MAN:603-604; RES:739-741).
    - Follow-ups: skip_035 105.8 → 103.3 ms; idx_score_v3, kb_rows (205 → 48 µs), top_k_rows (103 → 97.6 ms) (MAN:613-628).
  - **`apply_decode_small_kernels_040` plus `apply_bf16_twins_040`** (FN, generic CUDA/HIP):
    - Elementwise chains 8.4 → 2.7 µs; router 28 → 17 µs.
    - One conversation at 3K / 50K / 110K: -2.4 / -2.7 / -1.9 ms per token; MTP-off 25.9 → 27.3 tok/s (MAN:647-649; RES:874-875).
  - **`apply_ple_wake_041`** (FN, PLE reads from the SSD): gather 0.80 → 0.45 ms (MAN:652).
  - **`apply_parallel_sampling_035`**: eight conversations, sampled, 109.3 → 103.0 ms per step (MAN:615).
  - **IQ3_S matrix-core path** (iq3s-kernel snapshot): tg128 23.66 → 24.97 (+5.5%) and pp16384 903.64 → 947.37 (MAN:72-74).
  - **`apply_iq3s_mmq_hip`** (HIP): gate/up 73 → 156 GB/s at 32 tokens; eight users with MTP 60.5 → 70.1 tok/s (MAN:210; decode-budget.md:105).
  - **Multi-slot**:
    - `apply_multi_stream_qsa`: four users at 35K, 28.3 → 33–39 tok/s (decode-budget.md:108-117).
    - `apply_kv_regions`: MTP beside idle conversations, 32.8 → 38.5 tok/s (MAN:389).
    - `apply_qsa_active_blocks`: 47.6 → 44.8 ms (MAN:378).
    - Concurrency without MTP: 19.0 → 47.1 tok/s at 4 streams. With MTP: 37.5 / 48.9 / 57.7 tok/s for 1 / 2 / 4 streams (decode-budget.md:85-90).
  - **`apply_kv_q8_0`** (optional Q8_0 cache): K/V 3.2 GB instead of 6 at 262144 tokens, decode unchanged, prefill 1–2% slower (README:119).
  
  ## 4. Prefill [M]
  
  - **`apply_moe_glu3`** (IQ3_S gate/up rebuilt for gfx1151, where VALU and WMMA do not overlap): 35.9 → 19.9 ms per layer; 95.6K prefill 889.7–892.9 → 969.4 t/s (MAN:366-369; RES:193-203).
  - **`apply_prefill_kernels_020`**: HC inject fused into the combine-norm kernel, F32 GEMMs on WMMA instead of hipBLAS, a one-kernel indexer score, radix TOP_K, a 16-row GDN kernel. pp2048 GPU time 1860 → 1573 ms (2276 → 1788 at 64K); 95.6K prompt 992 → 1187 t/s (MAN:469; RES:295-299; README:117).
  - **`apply_prefill_043`**: shared-expert tail fused, XRES, norm+scale fused. 1K–16K prompts 920–1245 → 964–1301 t/s (MAN:676).
  - **`apply_hc_q8_fusions`**: first ubatch 7592 → 7245 ms (RES:184-186).
  - **`apply_gdn_r16_lds_029`**: GDN 3006 → 2582 ms at 64K. **`apply_norm_rows_plain_029`**: norms 449 → 352 ms (MAN:559-560).
  - **`apply_mmb_kq_042`**: Q4_K_XL prefill 875.9 → 1126.7 t/s (MAN:668).
  - **27B: `apply_qwen35_dense_prefill_050`**: K-quants on the MMB matrix-core path, +31–39%; pp2048 about 411 → 563 t/s (MAN:733; 27B:16).
  - **Disk / prompt cache and prefix cache**:
    - `apply_spc_direct_io`: 505 → 3482 MB/s; a full hit 18.1 → 8.1 s (MAN:301-304).
    - `apply_disk_restore_lazy`: 2724 → 734 ms (MAN:344).
    - `apply_prefix_cache_026`: agent workload 73.3K → 29.3K tokens processed, prompt time 172 → 60 s (MAN:526).
    - `apply_empty_slot_cache`: 186 → 7 s (MAN:400).
    - `apply_qwen35_multislot_051` (27B): 128K prefill beside other conversations 2009 → 874 s; decode 12.2 → 18.0 tok/s (MAN:734).
  
  ## 5. Applicability to the 27B
  
  - **Ablation [M]**: with every switch that fires on the 27B turned off, pp is about -1% and tg about -1.4%; no single switch shows above noise (27B:56-73).
  - **Static analysis [C], with no measurement**: QSA, HC, PLE, MoE kernels, IndexShare and the FA gather do not fire on the 27B (27B:109-144).
  - The 27B's MTP-off decode is already near the bandwidth limit: 12.4 t/s × 17.55 GB ≈ 218 GB/s (27B:13).
  
  ## 6. Dead ends (`docs/dead-ends.md`) [M]
  
  **Speculation**
  - Batching the per-query gather was neutral, 83.8 vs 83.6 ms. An apparent +10% turned out to be acceptance drift (:130-133).
  - Sparse attention on the draft context (`LLAMA_MTP_QSA_MIN_T=1`) was slower (:135-136, 186-188): 85.5 vs 85.1 ms per pass.
  - Folding the catch-up into the first draft step saved no time (:138-139).
  - FR-Spec vocabulary pruning to 64K tokens covers only 84–96% of text, because Chinese token ids are high (:141-143).
  - A draft window that catches up only the last 8K positions lost 4–7 points of acceptance (RES:1060-1062).
  - Draft precision (Q8_0 layer, Q6_K head) did not move acceptance (RES:902-905).
  - A per-step draft budget under load measured nothing (decode-budget.md:99).
  - A bf16 recurrent state measured nothing (decode-budget.md:100).
  
  **Kernels and quantisation**
  - Counting sort for expert ordering: -4% (:147-149).
  - Elementwise chain fusion: at most about 1 ms, within noise; kept anyway (:151-154).
  - IQ4_NL requantisation: +10–12% perplexity (:165-167).

# rulith-inference 的优化能否移植到 Strata（本机 3060M）

**结论：能直接带来提速的不多。** MTP 本身 Strata 已经有了，机制也基本一样。rulith 的大部分提速有两种：一种是 gfx1151（Strix Halo）专用的 HIP 内核，另一种的前提是全部权重都在 230 GB/s 的统一内存里。本机的瓶颈是 CPU 算专家（内存读约 55 GB/s）和 PCIe（26.8 GB/s），这两块 rulith 完全没有涉及。下面的数字都是 rulith 在 Strix Halo 上测的，不能直接换算到本机。

## Strata 已有、不用移植的

- **MTP 自投机解码。** rulith 用 Unsloth 的 MTP 附加文件，加 3 个草稿，Flash-Next 解码 22.3 → 38.7 tok/s。Strata 用自己从 BF16 检查点提取的 MTP 层，默认 `--spec 4`（1 个已接受 + 3 个草稿），本机接受率 61–92%。
- **验证后 GDN 状态的处理。** rulith 的 `gdn_deferred_rollback` 是验证时不写状态、提交时只重放接受的 token。Strata 的 `commit(n_keep)` 做的是同一件事。
- **CUDA graph、草稿词表裁剪、n-gram 查找草稿（`--suffix-draft`）**，都已经有了。

## 值得在本机试的，按成本从低到高

| 项目 | rulith 的实测 | Strata 现状 | 本机预期 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. 草稿长度按成本选** | MoE 上 3 个草稿最好；每多一个位置要多读约 10 个专家，草稿 4、5 个反而更慢 | 每个验证 token 路由到不同专家，CPU 要算这些专家的并集。T=2/3/4 时分别是单 token 的 1.75/2.4/3.05 倍，所以本机加草稿比 Halo 贵得多。控制器的成本模型默认值是在 RTX 5070 那台机器上测的 | **最先做**。只需改配置，A/B `--spec 3/4/5` 和 `--spec-min-p`，再按本机数据校准成本模型 |
| **2. temperature>0 时的投机采样** | 单会话 33.6 → 36.2 tok/s（+8%） | 已有，但默认关（`STRATA_SPEC_COUPLED=1`），本机没测过 | 只需测量 |
| **3. 低秩预打分的草稿头** | 草稿 2 个时 +3.6–4.9%；草稿头 338 → 135 MB，top-1 召回率 99.9% 以上 | Strata 用 `draft_vocab.bin` 子集。rulith 的 dead-ends 里记着：裁到 64K 词表只覆盖 84–96% 的文本，中文 token id 偏大，覆盖更差 | 先测子集的覆盖率。本机一轮里草稿步占比小，速度收益可能很小，主要看能不能提高中文接受率 |
| **4. 前缀缓存** | agent 负载下 prompt 时间 172 → 60 s | 按整轮保存，单轮变长后什么也复用不了（`cache_n` 0） | 对 BFCL 这类以 prefill 为主的负载，端到端收益可能最大。但这不是解码提速，GDN 状态又要靠检查点，工作量中等 |

## 不值得移植的

- **草稿注意力复用稀疏选择（`mtp_index_share`）。** 30K 上下文只快 0.6%，Strata 最大上下文 32K。
- **多会话 / 等长草稿。** Strata 只有单槽。多会话时 CPU 要算的专家并集更大，12 GB 显存也放不下多份 KV。只有确实要同时服务多个会话才考虑。
- **glu3、IQ3_S MMQ、mmvq_i8、WMMA prefill 等内核。** 都是 gfx1151 专用，或者改的是 ggml 计算图，和 Strata 自己的 CUDA 引擎对不上。

## 本机更大的提速空间（rulith 帮不上）

- **每 token 解码时间拆分还没测过。** GPU 稠密层、CPU 专家、PCIe、同步各占多少都不知道。工具已经有：`STRATA_VERIFY_PROFILE=1`、`--stage-timing`。不先测这个，上面每一项的收益都只能猜。
- **`--pcie-frac` 引擎默认值仍是 0.55。** 实测最好是 0–0.25，快 20–30%。现在只在配置里改了，引擎的选择规则没改。
- **UD-IQ4_XS 的 CPU 内核问题。** 它的 IQ4_XS gate/up 和 Q8_0 down 在 CPU 上走单 token 的 ggml 内核，验证多个 token 时吃不到多 token 内核的 2–2.4 倍加速。它的 GPU 专家命中率只有 48%（Coder 是 65%）。

建议顺序：先测每 token 时间拆分，再 A/B 草稿长度和投机采样。这三项都不用改代码，测完再决定 3、4 值不值得做。要我现在跑吗？

另外，当前工作区在 `rulith` 分支上，不在 `3060M`；这次只读，没改任何文件。
好，先测每 token 时间拆分

with a message; #403: a clamped budget no longer fails the safety check that follows, and a budget that cannot be
kept at all is a warning, with every expert read from the files). Setup sets N with `--resident-budget-gib N`. With
the GGUF read in place it also warms the next layer's likely experts: while the CPU works on a layer, a thread applies
the next layer's router to this layer's input and asks the OS for the pages of the predicted experts that neither the
GPU nor the RAM budget holds (only pages - the experts computed are the same; `STRATA_LOOKAHEAD=0` turns it off). This
is what runs [Unsloth's UD-Q4_K_XL](UNSLOTH_Q4.md) (72 GiB of experts) on a 64 GB PC: 7-8.5 tokens/s at N = 40 on an
RTX 5070, against ~3 tokens/s before these changes.

**How much came from where:** with `--stats` the engine prints the tiers of the decode (`expert tiers`: blobs from the
RAM copy, blobs and MB from the files, the time spent reading them; `routing prefetch`: how many of the file reads had
been warmed). The server log has the same per request (`expert tiers: GPU ... hits ...; RAM ... blobs, files ...
blobs ... MB read`), and `GET /metrics` lists `ram_blobs`, `file_blobs` and `file_mb` for each recent request (with
engine 0.1.31 or newer).

Time to first token is prompt length / prompt speed: with Q2_0 about 4 s at 4K, 25 s at 32K, under 2 minutes at 128K
and 4.5 minutes at 262K (engine 0.1.13 made long prompts about twice as fast, below).

**Faster prompts (engine 0.1.13):** the prompt is read in chunks of up to 8,192 tokens instead of 2,048 (`--prefill

kept at all is a warning, with every expert read from the files). Setup sets N with `--resident-budget-gib N`. With
the GGUF read in place it also warms the next layer's likely experts: while the CPU works on a layer, a thread applies
the next layer's router to this layer's input and asks the OS for the pages of the predicted experts that neither the
GPU nor the RAM budget holds (only pages - the experts computed are the same; `STRATA_LOOKAHEAD=0` turns it off). This
is what runs [Unsloth's UD-Q4_K_XL](UNSLOTH_Q4.md) (72 GiB of experts) on a 64 GB PC: 7-8.5 tokens/s at N = 40 on an

been warmed). The server log has the same per request (`expert tiers: GPU ... hits ...; RAM ... blobs, files ...

engine 0.1.31 or newer).

kept at all is a warning, with every expert read from the files). Setup sets N with `--resident-budget-gib N`. With
the GGUF read in place it also warms the next layer's likely experts: while the CPU works on a layer, a thread applies
the next layer's router to this layer's input and asks the OS for the pages of the predicted experts that neither the
GPU nor the RAM budget holds (only pages - the experts computed are the same; `STRATA_LOOKAHEAD=0` turns it off). This
is what runs [Unsloth's UD-Q4_K_XL](UNSLOTH_Q4.md) (72 GiB of experts) on a 64 GB PC: 7-8.5 tokens/s at N = 40 on an
RTX 5070, against ~3 tokens/s before these changes.

**How much came from where:** with `--stats` the engine prints the tiers of the decode (`expert tiers`: blobs from the
RAM copy, blobs and MB from the files, the time spent reading them; `routing prefetch`: how many of the file reads had
been warmed). The server log has the same per request (`expert tiers: GPU ... hits ...; RAM ... blobs, files ...
blobs ... MB read`), and `GET /metrics` lists `ram_blobs`, `file_blobs` and `file_mb` for each recent request (with
engine 0.1.31 or newer).

and 4.5 minutes at 262K (engine 0.1.13 made long prompts about twice as fast, below).


Result: 1079 tensors, 302 served natively, arena 1.37 GiB; `tokenizer/` with a vocabulary of 248320. The low-RAM

## 6. The MTP draft layer

The draft layer for speculative decoding comes from the original Qwen checkpoint (only its MTP tensors, 4.9 GB):

```sh
M=../Strata-data/mtp
python tools/mtp_fetch.py fetch --out $M
python tools/mtp_pack.py --src $M --experts q2_0 --out $M/mtp-q2_0.gguf
python tools/mtp_rt.py --gguf $M/mtp-q2_0.gguf --out $M/rt
cp data/draft_vocab.bin $M/rt/draft_vocab.bin     # setup's default subset (cjk)
```

## 7. The config and the start script

`strata-coder-iq1_m.json` carries the arguments setup chooses for this PC: 32K context (recommended for 12 GB
VRAM), 8-bit KV cache, no images, no KV streaming (it starts at 64K), no low-RAM mode. Shard 2 holds the
`per_layer_token_embd` table, so it is the `--ple-gguf`:

```json
          "--mtp", "/home/luwei/work/AI/Strata-data/mtp/rt",

 "cwd": "/home/luwei/work/AI/Strata",
 "tokenizer": "/home/luwei/work/AI/Strata-data/packs/coder-iq1_m/tokenizer",
 "model_name": "qwen3.8-flash-next-coder-iq1_m",
 "log": "/home/luwei/work/AI/Strata/strata-coder-iq1_m.log",

}
```

import json, subprocess, sys, time, urllib.request
from pathlib import Path
S = Path(__file__).parent; ROOT = Path("/home/luwei/work/AI/Strata"); URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8080"
base, label, fracs = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3:]
E = Path("/mnt/evox2/large/work/AI/EngramHalo.cpp/src")
L = (E / "llama-model-loader.cpp").read_text()
i = L.index("static std::vector<std::string> llama_get_list_splits"); j = L.index("\n}\n", i) + 3
DECODE = "Rewrite this C++ function to be clearer and faster. Keep the behavior. Reply with the code.\n\n```cpp\n" + L[i:j] + "```"
SRC = "".join(p.read_text() for p in sorted(E.glob("llama-*.cpp")) if p.name != "llama-model-loader.cpp")

def post(path, body):
    r = urllib.request.Request(URL + path, json.dumps(body).encode(), {"Content-Type": "application/json"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(r, timeout=3600) as f:
        return json.load(f)
def chat(text, n):
    return post("/v1/chat/completions", {"model": "x", "temperature": 0, "max_tokens": n,
            "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": text}]})
def count(text):
    return post("/v1/messages/count_tokens", {"model": "x", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": text}]})["input_tokens"]
def cut(text, tokens):
    n = int(len(text) * tokens / count(text[:400000]) * len(text[:400000]) / len(text)) if False else int(tokens * 3.3)
    for _ in range(4):
        c = count(text[:n])
        if abs(c - tokens) <= tokens * 0.01: break
        n = int(n * tokens / c)
    return text[:n]

texts = None
for x in fracs:
    c = json.load(open(ROOT / base)); c["args"] += ["--pcie-frac", x]; c["log"] = str(S / f"ab-{label}-{x}-engine.log")
    cfg = S / f"ab-{label}-{x}.json"; cfg.write_text(json.dumps(c))
    log = open(S / f"ab-{label}-{x}-server.log", "w")
    p = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, "serve/server.py", "--engine", "strata", "--config", str(cfg), "--port", "8080"],
                         cwd=ROOT, stdout=log, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT)
    t0 = time.time()
    while "ready: http" not in (S / f"ab-{label}-{x}-server.log").read_text():
        if p.poll() is not None: sys.exit(f"server died at {x}")
        time.sleep(1)
    ready = round(time.time() - t0)
    args = subprocess.run(["bash", "-c", "ps -o args= -p $(pgrep -x strata) | grep -oE -- '--pcie-frac [0-9.]+'"],
                          capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip()
    if texts is None:                       # the same prefill texts for every value (a fresh server each time)
        a = cut(SRC, 4096); b = cut(SRC[len(a):], 16384); texts = (a, b)
    chat("Write a thread-safe LRU cache in C++.", 128)                       # warm-up
    for k in range(3):
        t = chat(DECODE, 512)["timings"]
        print(json.dumps({"model": label, "pcie_frac": x, "engine_args": args, "test": f"decode#{k+1}",
                          "tok_s": t["predicted_per_second"], "tokens": t["predicted_n"],
                          "drafts": f'{t.get("draft_n_accepted")}/{t.get("draft_n")}', "cache_n": t["cache_n"]}), flush=True)
    for name, text in (("prefill 4K", texts[0]), ("prefill 16K", texts[1])):
        t = chat(text, 1)["timings"]
        print(json.dumps({"model": label, "pcie_frac": x, "test": name, "tok_s": t["prompt_per_second"],
                          "tokens": t["prompt_n"], "cache_n": t["cache_n"], "ready_s": ready}), flush=True)
    p.terminate(); p.wait()
    while subprocess.run(["pgrep", "-x", "strata"], capture_output=True).returncode == 0: time.sleep(1)

S=/tmp/claude-1000/-home-luwei-work-AI-Strata/7383c513-d686-461b-b02e-39b288fc437e/scratchpad/split; python3 - $S <<'EOF'
import re,sys
S=sys.argv[1]
CAT={"proj":["q8+qkv/q-idx gemv","z","out-proj","q8+kv-idx","q+q-idx"],
     "mix":["conv","ab","rec","k/v+norm-rope","kv+idx append","scores+topk","kv-resolve","attention","gate"],
     "hc":["hc0 norm","hc0 down","hc0 up","hc-read1+router"],"shared":["shared+quant"],"vram":["VRAM hits"],
     "pcie":["PCIe grp"],"wait":["waitA","waitB","waitCPU"],"comb":["copy+combine","(gap)"],"head":["head"]}
names=sorted({n for v in CAT.values() for n in v},key=len,reverse=True)
for m in ["coder","ud"]:
    L=open(f"{S}/{m}-profile-engine.log").read().splitlines()
    st=[l for l in L if "GPU stages" in l][-2:]; dt=[l for l in L if "decode timing:" in l][-2:]
    tl=[l for l in open(f"{S}/{m}-timing-engine.log").read().splitlines() if "decode timing:" in l][-2:]
    acc={k:0 for k in CAT}
    for l in st:
        body=l.split(":",1)[1].split("| total")[0]
        for k,v in CAT.items():
            for n in v:
                for x in re.findall(r"(?:^|\s)"+re.escape(n)+r" ([0-9.]+)",body): acc[k]+=float(x)/2
    def f(l,key): return float(re.search(key+r" ([0-9.]+)",l).group(1))
    for name,lines in [("timing",tl),("profile",dt)]:
        w=sum(f(l,"=")if False else float(re.search(r"([0-9.]+) ms/window",l).group(1)) for l in lines)/2
        tpw=sum(float(re.search(r"([0-9.]+) tokens/window",l).group(1)) for l in lines)/2
        ver=sum(f(l,"verify") for l in lines)/2; dr=sum(f(l,"draft") for l in lines)/2
        wt=sum(f(l,"GPU-reach wait") for l in lines)/2; cpu=sum(f(l,"CPU") for l in lines)/2
        ce=sum(float(re.search(r"CPU experts ([0-9.]+)",l).group(1)) for l in lines)/2
        hits=sum(float(re.search(r"VRAM hits ([0-9.]+)",l).group(1)) for l in lines)/2
        pc=sum(float(re.search(r"PCIe ([0-9.]+)\s*$",l).group(1)) for l in lines)/2
        print(f"{m} {name}: window {w:.2f} ms, {tpw:.2f} tok/window -> {w/tpw:.2f} ms/token; verify {ver:.2f} (host GPU-wait {wt:.2f}, CPU {cpu:.2f}); draft {dr:.2f}; per layer: CPU experts {ce:.2f}, VRAM {hits:.2f}, PCIe {pc:.2f}")
    tot=sum(acc.values()); print(m,"GPU", {k:round(v,2) for k,v in acc.items()}, "total",round(tot,2))
EOF

**A draft** (`src/program/generate.cpp`, 2026-10-04, compiled; not yet run in the engine - the GPU was busy):

- `probe_host_read_gbps(threads)`: the host RAM read bandwidth with the pool's thread count (one per physical core),
  a 1 GiB buffer, best of 3 passes; about 0.3 s at start, only when the share is not given.
- `default_pcie_frac(native, link, host)`: one function for both places the rule was written. The link-only rule
  is unchanged. With `STRATA_PCIE_HOST_RULE=1` it also weighs the link against the host:
  `0.55 x (link / host) / (27 / 44.14)` - the measuring machine's link-to-kernel ratio - and never raises the value.
- The probe line now also prints the host bandwidth: "PCIe probe: 26.8 GB/s host->device, host RAM read X GB/s ->
  pcie_frac ...", so starts on other PCs collect both numbers.

Tested on its own (the two functions compiled into a small program, 2026-10-04, while a BFCL run used the GPU and
RAM): the probe read **45.0 GB/s** with 15 threads (55 GB/s idle with the STREAM test above); rule off: 0.55 / 0.28 /
0 for a 26.8 / 13 / 2 GB/s link, as before; rule on: **0.54** at 26.8 GB/s and 45 GB/s, 0.44 with 55 GB/s, 0.55 for
the measuring machine's numbers, 0.21 for a 13 GB/s link; the canonical pack keeps 0.2.

**So the ratio is not the explanation.** Weighing the link against RAM bandwidth moves the share from 0.55 to
0.44-0.54 on this PC; the measured best is 0-0.25. What the draft does not measure is what most likely differs:
the pool's own expert throughput (15 workers here, 5 there; the IQ kernels may be limited by compute, not only by
RAM) and the GPU's side of the copies (the copy kernel runs on the GPU's SMs: 30 on this GPU, 48 on an RTX 5070).
That is why the rule stays opt-in. Next measurement, when the GPU is free: decode at `--pcie-frac` 0 and 0.55 with
the engine's pool counters (`pool phases ... drain`) and the GPU's per-token times, to see which side waits. The
alternatives to a formula: let setup run `--calibrate` also with `--yes`, or balance the share at run time from
the measured drain and copy times (the share is already settable per request: `strata_tune` key `pcie_frac`).

- `probe_host_read_gbps(threads)`: the host RAM read bandwidth with the pool's thread count (one per physical core),
  a 1 GiB buffer, best of 3 passes; about 0.3 s at start, only when the share is not given.
- `default_pcie_frac(native, link, host)`: one function for both places the rule was written. The link-only rule
  is unchanged. With `STRATA_PCIE_HOST_RULE=1` it also weighs the link against the host:
  `0.55 x (link / host) / (27 / 44.14)` - the measuring machine's link-to-kernel ratio - and never raises the value.
- The probe line now also prints the host bandwidth: "PCIe probe: 26.8 GB/s host->device, host RAM read X GB/s ->
  pcie_frac ...", so starts on other PCs collect both numbers.

Tested on its own (the two functions compiled into a small program, 2026-10-04, while a BFCL run used the GPU and
RAM): the probe read **45.0 GB/s** with 15 threads (55 GB/s idle with the STREAM test above); rule off: 0.55 / 0.28 /
0 for a 26.8 / 13 / 2 GB/s link, as before; rule on: **0.54** at 26.8 GB/s and 45 GB/s, 0.44 with 55 GB/s, 0.55 for
the measuring machine's numbers, 0.21 for a 13 GB/s link; the canonical pack keeps 0.2.

**So the ratio is not the explanation.** Weighing the link against RAM bandwidth moves the share from 0.55 to
0.44-0.54 on this PC; the measured best is 0-0.25. What the draft does not measure is what most likely differs:
the pool's own expert throughput (15 workers here, 5 there; the IQ kernels may be limited by compute, not only by
RAM) and the GPU's side of the copies (the copy kernel runs on the GPU's SMs: 30 on this GPU, 48 on an RTX 5070).
That is why the rule stays opt-in. Next measurement, when the GPU is free: decode at `--pcie-frac` 0 and 0.55 with
the engine's pool counters (`pool phases ... drain`) and the GPU's per-token times, to see which side waits. The
alternatives to a formula: let setup run `--calibrate` also with `--yes`, or balance the share at run time from
the measured drain and copy times (the share is already settable per request: `strata_tune` key `pcie_frac`).

cat >> docs/3060M.md <<'EOF'

## Where the decode time goes (2026-10-17)

The measurement the section above asked for. The same prompt and procedure as the `--pcie-frac` A/B (a fresh
server per run, a warm-up, the C++ rewrite request three times, temperature 0, about 230 tokens out), the configs in
the repository root (`--pcie-frac` 0.2 for the Coder, 0.25 for UD-IQ4_XS), two runs per model: one with
`STRATA_DECODE_TIMING=1` (the host's view of each verify window), one adding `STRATA_VERIFY_PROFILE=1` (GPU
timestamps per stage and layer). Script and raw lines: `benchmarks/2026-10-17-3060m-decode-split.py` and `.log`.

Decode in the timing run: Coder 61.5 / 64.3 / 62.2 tokens/s (the A/B: 62.3), UD-IQ4_XS 55.4 / 54.7 / 56.0 (the
A/B: 55.4); the profile run 58.8 / 63.3 / 62.4 and 54.8 / 54.3 / 55.5, its windows 0.6-0.7 ms (1%) longer. The
numbers below are the mean of decodes 2 and 3 (decode 1 had more prompt-lookup windows: avg T 4.52 against 3.94).

**The host's view** (ms per verify window; a window commits the accepted drafts plus one token):

| | Coder IQ1_M | UD-IQ4_XS |
|---|---|---|
| window | 58.6 | 69.8 |
| tokens committed per window (avg window T) | 3.70 (3.94) | 3.87 (4.15) |
| **ms per token** | **15.8** | **18.1** |
| verify | 53.3 | 64.6 |
| - the host waits for the GPU to reach a layer | 32.8 | 27.3 |
| - CPU experts (the pool's drain, host thread included) | 16.4 | 33.0 |
| - plan, queue, jobs, staging | 1.0 | 1.1 |
| MTP draft | 5.2 | 5.2 |
| commit + emit | 0.04 | 0.04 |
| experts per layer and window: on the CPU / VRAM hits / over PCIe | 7.8 / 28.6 / 1.2 | 12.2 / 22.3 / 3.6 |

**The GPU's view** (the profile run, ms per window, the 48 layers summed; the stages' sum is the verify time):

| GPU stage | Coder IQ1_M | UD-IQ4_XS |
|---|---|---|
| projections: q/k/v/z GEMVs, out-proj, the indexer's q | 10.7 | 10.2 |
| hyper-connection reads (norm, down, up) + router | 14.0 | 10.6 |
| GDN conv / gates / recurrence + QSA K/V, scores, attention | 2.9 | 2.9 |
| shared expert + activation quantization | 2.0 | 1.9 |
| experts in VRAM | 11.2 | 9.5 |
| experts copied over PCIe (their group kernel) | 2.0 | 3.5 |
| copy + combine | 0.9 | 1.1 |
| LM head | 3.0 | 3.1 |
| **waiting for the CPU** (waitA + waitB + waitCPU) | **7.6** | **22.8** |
| total | 54.3 | 65.5 |

- **The Coder is GPU-bound.** The GPU computes 46.7 ms of the 58.6 ms window and waits 7.6 ms for the CPU; the
  CPU experts' 16.4 ms run mostly beside the GPU's VRAM hits. The largest GPU items are the hyper-connection reads
  with the router (14.0 ms, 24% of the window), the VRAM experts (11.2) and the projections (10.7).
- **UD-IQ4_XS is CPU-bound.** The GPU waits 22.8 ms per window (33% of it) for 12.2 CPU experts per layer, against
  7.8 for the Coder: fewer of its experts fit in VRAM (1864 against 2666) and 0.25 of the misses go over PCIe.
- **The projections are not limited by bytes**: UD-IQ4_XS's native projection matrices are 2975 MiB, the Coder's
  2019 MiB, and both take 10.2-10.7 ms. An estimate of the GPU's bandwidth floor: if every loaded weight (1406 +
  2019 MiB for the Coder) and every VRAM hit (28.6 x 48 experts of about 2.06 MB, the cache's 5.11 GiB / 2666
  slots) is read once per window, that is 6.4 GB, 19 ms at 336 GB/s, against 46.7 ms of GPU work: about 40%.
- **The CPU experts run near the RAM's bandwidth**, an estimate with the same average expert size: Coder 7.8 x 48
  x 2.06 MB in 16.4 ms = 47 GB/s, UD-IQ4_XS 12.2 x 48 x 2.41 MB (4.19 GiB / 1864 slots) in 33.0 ms = 43 GB/s,
  against 55 GB/s read with 15 threads (STREAM test above). Not the codebook-bound 5 GB/s per core of
  `native_expert.cpp:81`: at most about 20-30% is left for faster CPU kernels.
- The hyper-connection + router stage is 3.4 ms longer for the Coder (the `hc-read1+router` part: 9.0 against 5.6
  ms); not explained yet.
- The MTP draft is 5.2 ms per window (9% of the Coder's, 7% of UD-IQ4_XS's); how much of it is the draft head is
  not measured.
EOF

+The measurement the section above asked for. The same prompt and procedure as the `--pcie-frac` A/B (a fresh
